Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{5}^{1}\,f(x)\,\text{d}x=2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factoring out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}(f(x)+4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{5}f(x)\,\text{d}x+4{\int }_{1}^{5}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2+4\cdot {\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,|}_{1}^{5} \\  & =2+2({5}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =2+48 \\  & =50.\end{aligned}
$$
